title: Scan-to-BIM explained: from laser scanning to an accurate as-built model
excerpt: Learn how Scan-to-BIM converts laser-scanned point clouds into 3D BIM models, what affects accuracy, and how to plan project deliverables.
body:
A practical guide to capturing existing conditions and turning site measurements into usable BIM information.

Renovating an existing building, upgrading its systems or planning new work inside an operating facility requires reliable information about current site conditions. Yet original drawings may be missing, outdated or different from what was actually built.

**Scan-to-BIM** helps address this challenge by using reality-capture data, such as laser scans, to develop a Building Information Modelling (BIM) model of existing conditions.

The process can provide project teams with a measurable digital reference for planning, coordination, refurbishment and asset documentation. However, the quality of the final model depends on the scanning plan, site conditions, processing methods, modelling requirements and quality checks.

This guide explains how Scan-to-BIM works, what affects accuracy, which deliverables to define and how to plan a project around its intended use.

## What is Scan-to-BIM?
Scan-to-BIM is the process of capturing the physical conditions of a building or infrastructure asset and using the resulting data to create a BIM model.

A common approach uses laser scanning to collect millions of measured points from surfaces. These points form a **point cloud**, which represents the geometry of the scanned environment. The point cloud is then processed and used as a reference for creating selected model elements.

Depending on the project, those elements may include walls, floors, columns, beams, ceilings, ducts, pipes, equipment and other visible components.

The model is not automatically created in full detail simply because a scan exists. The required elements, level of geometric development, information fields and acceptance criteria must be defined for the intended use.

> **In simple terms:** Scan-to-BIM turns measured information about an existing site into a structured digital model that project teams can use for defined design, coordination or asset-information tasks.

## When is Scan-to-BIM useful?
Scan-to-BIM is particularly useful when teams need dependable information about existing conditions and cannot rely on drawings alone.

- **Building renovation:** Capture existing geometry before designing alterations.
- **MEP upgrades:** Document visible mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems to support coordination.
- **Facility documentation:** Develop a digital record of selected building elements and spaces.
- **Extension or retrofit projects:** Understand interfaces between existing structures and proposed work.
- **Heritage and complex structures:** Record irregular shapes and architectural features where appropriate scanning methods can capture them.
- **As-built documentation:** Compare captured conditions with available drawings or design information, using agreed verification procedures.

Suitability depends on access, required detail, safety conditions, project scope and whether the relevant surfaces and assets can be captured.

## The Scan-to-BIM workflow: 6 key steps
### 1. Define the project requirements
Start by identifying how the model will be used. A model for early renovation planning may need different detail from one used for MEP coordination or asset handover.

Agree on the areas to be surveyed, the elements to be modelled, required accuracy, expected model development, information fields, delivery formats and acceptance criteria. Also identify any areas that cannot be accessed or scanned.

### 2. Plan the site survey
The survey plan determines where scanning equipment will be positioned and how scan coverage will be achieved. The team should consider site access, line of sight, reflective or transparent surfaces, obstructions, lighting where relevant to the capture method, operational restrictions and safety.

For larger or complex sites, multiple scan positions may be required. Survey control or reference points may also be used where the project requires the scan data to align with a known coordinate system.

### 3. Capture the existing conditions
Laser scanners collect spatial measurements from visible surfaces. Depending on the project, other reality-capture methods such as photogrammetry may complement the survey.

Coverage and data quality should be checked while the team is on site. Missing areas, obstructed equipment or insufficient detail may require additional capture before the survey is considered complete.

### 4. Register and process the point cloud
When several scans are collected, they may need to be aligned or registered into a common coordinate system. The data is then reviewed and processed for issues such as incomplete coverage, noise, stray points or alignment errors.

The project team should confirm how the processed data will be referenced and delivered, including any required coordinate system, units and file formats.

### 5. Develop the BIM model
Modellers use the processed point cloud as a reference to create the agreed BIM elements. Depending on the scope, the model may include architectural, structural or MEP components.

Not every scanned point becomes a model element. The team should model what is required for the agreed purpose and document any assumptions, exclusions or elements that could not be verified.

### 6. Validate and deliver the model
The final model should be checked against the agreed requirements. Validation may include comparing model geometry with the point cloud, reviewing coverage and checking required model attributes.

Deliverables should be reviewed for completeness, file compatibility, naming conventions and any project-specific acceptance criteria before handover.

## What affects Scan-to-BIM accuracy?
Accuracy is not determined by the scanner alone. It depends on the full workflow, from field capture to model validation.

### Scanner capability and settings
Equipment specifications, operating range, measurement conditions and selected settings influence the captured data.

### Survey planning and scan coverage
Occluded areas and limited lines of sight can leave gaps. A good survey plan helps reduce missed surfaces.

### Registration and alignment
Errors when combining multiple scans can affect the overall point cloud and the model created from it.

### Site conditions and surface properties
Reflective, transparent, dark or difficult-to-access surfaces may affect capture quality depending on the equipment and method.

### Modelling decisions
The modeller interprets point-cloud data to create defined elements. Simplification, assumptions and the agreed model scope influence how closely the model represents the captured conditions.

### Quality assurance
Clear tolerances, suitable checks and documented acceptance criteria help determine whether the final deliverable meets the project requirements.

> **Important:** No single accuracy figure applies to every Scan-to-BIM project. The required tolerance, and the method used to verify it, should be agreed according to the project's needs and the capabilities of the survey and modelling workflow.

## Point cloud vs BIM model: What is the difference?
A point cloud and a BIM model are related, but they are not the same deliverable.

### Point cloud
- A collection of measured points representing captured surfaces.
- Primarily records captured geometry and visible conditions.
- Useful as a reference for measurement, verification and modelling.
- May contain noise, gaps or points from temporary objects.

### BIM model
- A structured digital representation made from model elements.
- Can include geometry plus structured element properties and information.
- Useful for defined design, coordination, documentation and asset-information tasks.
- Requires interpretation, modelling decisions and validation against the agreed scope.

A point cloud is often a key source for the model, but it does not replace a properly scoped and validated BIM deliverable.

## What deliverables should be agreed before the project starts?
The deliverables should match the project's intended use. Depending on the agreed scope, a Scan-to-BIM package may include:

- Registered or processed point-cloud files.
- A BIM model covering the agreed building areas and elements.
- Specified model formats and any required exchange formats.
- Agreed coordinate system, units and reference information.
- Required element properties or asset data, if included in scope.
- Quality-check results or a record of verification against agreed tolerances.
- A list of exclusions, inaccessible areas, assumptions and known limitations.

These items are not automatically included in every Scan-to-BIM service. They should be defined in the project scope, along with the expected level of model development, delivery schedule and acceptance criteria.

## What affects the cost of Scan-to-BIM?
Scan-to-BIM costs vary because each site and deliverable has different requirements. Important cost drivers can include:

- **Site size and complexity:** Larger or more complex environments may require more survey positions and processing.
- **Access and operating restrictions:** Limited access, occupied spaces or restricted working hours can affect survey planning.
- **Required accuracy:** Tighter tolerances may require more careful control, capture and verification.
- **Model scope:** The number and type of elements to be modelled affect modelling effort.
- **Required LOD and information:** More developed geometry and additional asset data may increase the work involved.
- **Deliverable formats and coordination:** Special exchange requirements, validation reports or integration with existing project data can affect scope.
- **Programme:** Short deadlines or phased deliverables may affect resourcing and planning.

A reliable quotation should be based on the survey area, site conditions, modelling scope, required accuracy, deliverable formats and schedule, not simply the floor area alone.

## Common Scan-to-BIM mistakes to avoid
- Starting the survey without agreeing on the intended use of the model.
- Assuming that scanning every visible area is always possible.
- Treating a point cloud as if it were already a complete BIM model.
- Combining scans without checking registration quality and coordinate alignment.
- Requesting a high level of model detail without defining which elements require it.
- Failing to document inaccessible areas, assumptions or exclusions.
- Accepting the model without agreed validation criteria.
- Promising a specific accuracy level without a defined measurement and verification method.

Clear scope definition, careful survey planning and documented quality checks help reduce avoidable rework.

## How to select a Scan-to-BIM provider
When evaluating a provider, project teams should look beyond the equipment or software being used. Ask how the provider will meet the project's actual requirements.

- What survey method and equipment are proposed, and why are they suitable for the site?
- How will scan coverage, registration and coordinate alignment be checked?
- What accuracy or tolerance can be supported, and how will it be verified?
- Which elements will be modelled, and what will be excluded?
- What model development level and information fields are included?
- What formats will be delivered, and can they be used within the project's workflow?
- Will the provider document assumptions, limitations and quality checks?
- Can relevant examples be shared with permission and without disclosing confidential project details?

Evaluate the answers against the project scope and evidence supplied. Avoid relying on unsupported performance claims or project examples that have not been approved for disclosure.

## Frequently asked questions
### 1. What is Scan-to-BIM?
Scan-to-BIM is the process of capturing an existing physical environment, often with laser scanning, and using the resulting data to create a BIM model for a defined purpose.

### 2. What is a point cloud in Scan-to-BIM?
A point cloud is a collection of measured spatial points that represent visible surfaces captured during a survey. It is commonly used as a reference for developing and checking a BIM model.

### 3. Is a point cloud the same as a BIM model?
No. A point cloud contains captured measurement data, while a BIM model contains structured model elements and may include additional properties and information.

### 4. How accurate is Scan-to-BIM?
Accuracy varies with equipment, survey planning, site conditions, scan registration, modelling methods and verification. The required tolerance should be defined for each project and checked using an agreed method.

### 5. How long does a Scan-to-BIM project take?
Duration depends on site size, access, complexity, scan coverage, model scope, required detail and deliverables. A timeline should be estimated after reviewing these factors.

### 6. What files are delivered in a Scan-to-BIM project?
Deliverables may include processed point clouds, BIM model files, exchange formats and quality-check information. The exact package depends on the agreed scope.

### 7. Can Scan-to-BIM be used for MEP coordination?
Yes, when the survey captures the relevant systems and the model is developed to the required scope and accuracy. Hidden or inaccessible services may require other records or investigation.

### 8. What affects Scan-to-BIM cost?
Key factors include site size and complexity, access, required accuracy, model scope, level of development, asset information, file formats and schedule.

## Conclusion
Scan-to-BIM provides a practical way to turn measured information about existing buildings and infrastructure into a structured digital model. It can support renovation, coordination, documentation and asset-information tasks when the model is developed for a clear purpose.

A successful project starts by defining the required areas, elements, accuracy, information and deliverables. It then relies on a planned survey, careful point-cloud processing, suitable modelling and validation against agreed criteria.

The goal is not simply to create a detailed model. It is to deliver reliable, usable information that meets the needs of the project team.

title: Adopting BIM in projects: is cost really the biggest barrier?
excerpt: Is cost really the biggest barrier to BIM adoption? We break down where BIM truly delivers value and how to approach it project-first.
body:
Building Information Modelling, or BIM, has become an increasingly important part of digital construction. Yet despite its growing adoption, many project teams still hesitate to introduce BIM into their projects. One of the most common concerns is straightforward: "How much will BIM add to the project cost?" It is a reasonable question. BIM adoption can require investment in software, skilled professionals, training, processes, and technology. For companies working within tight project budgets, these additional requirements can appear difficult to justify, particularly when traditional design and construction workflows are already in place. But there is another question worth asking: "What does it cost when project information is poorly coordinated?" That is where the BIM conversation becomes more interesting.

Building Information Modelling, or BIM, has become an increasingly important part of digital construction. Yet despite its growing adoption, many project teams still hesitate to introduce BIM into their projects.

One of the most common concerns is straightforward:

> “How much will BIM add to the project cost?”

It is a reasonable question.

BIM adoption can require investment in software, skilled professionals, training, processes, and technology. For companies working within tight project budgets, these additional requirements can appear difficult to justify, particularly when traditional design and construction workflows are already in place.

But there is another question worth asking:

> **What does it cost when project information is poorly coordinated?**

That is where the BIM conversation becomes more interesting.

## The real challenge is not simply the cost of BIM

BIM should not be viewed as simply purchasing software or creating a 3D model.

Modern BIM is increasingly understood as a collaborative process for managing project information, coordination, and data across different stages of a project. The 2025 NBS Digital Construction Report, based on responses from 559 design and construction professionals, found that BIM adoption remained strong while industry understanding continued to move beyond the idea of BIM being simply a “3D model with data.”

This distinction matters.

A BIM workflow can involve architectural, structural, MEP and other project information being brought together so that teams can identify issues, communicate changes, and make decisions using a more coordinated information environment.

So the cost discussion should not stop at:

> “How much does BIM cost?”

It should also consider:

> **“What problems are we trying to prevent or manage through better coordination and information?”**

## Why do companies hesitate to adopt BIM?

Cost is certainly one of the barriers.

Research and industry surveys have identified several recurring challenges, including the cost of implementation, lack of in-house expertise, training requirements, and resistance to changing established workflows. NBS has previously identified cost, expertise, and training among the barriers reported by professionals considering BIM adoption.

For a company that has never used BIM extensively, the initial investment may include:

- BIM software and technology
- Hiring or outsourcing BIM professionals
- Training existing project teams
- Developing new workflows and standards
- Coordinating information between multiple disciplines
- Establishing processes for managing project data

For smaller projects or companies with limited resources, these considerations can understandably create hesitation.

However, treating BIM as a single upfront expense can provide an incomplete picture.

## The cost of poor coordination

Construction projects involve numerous disciplines working together.

Architecture, structure, HVAC, plumbing, electrical systems, fire protection and other services must eventually coexist within the same physical environment.

When information between these disciplines is not properly coordinated, problems can emerge during construction.

A duct may conflict with a structural element.

A pipe may occupy the same space required by a cable tray.

A ceiling may not have enough space for all the required services.

A design revision may not reach every team at the right time.

These problems can result in rework, changes, delays, additional coordination meetings, material changes, and other project disruptions.

BIM does not eliminate these risks automatically. However, it can provide a structured environment in which potential conflicts and coordination issues can be identified earlier.

Recent research reviewing BIM investment value has identified areas such as reduction of changes and rework, improved productivity, fewer requests for information, schedule efficiency, and improved coordination among the factors commonly studied when evaluating BIM's financial value.

A 2025 systematic review of 4D BIM research similarly identified visualization, communication and coordination, scheduling, and construction progress monitoring among the most frequently reported benefit areas.

A key point is that BIM is not simply about producing a model. Its value can come from how project teams use coordinated information to support decisions throughout the project.

## BIM is not a guarantee of cost savings

This is an important point.

It would be misleading to present BIM as a technology that automatically makes every project cheaper.

The financial value of BIM depends on many factors, including project size, complexity, implementation quality, team capability, scope, and the stage at which BIM is introduced.

Researchers have also pointed out that there is currently no standardized method for calculating BIM ROI across projects. Different studies measure different benefits, making direct comparisons difficult.

That means the business case for BIM should be built around the specific project.

For example, a highly complex hospital, airport, commercial development, or mixed-use project with extensive MEP coordination may have very different BIM requirements from a small, relatively simple building.

The question is therefore not whether BIM has a universal return.

The better question is whether BIM provides sufficient value for the risks, complexity, and coordination requirements of a particular project.

## Start with the project, not the technology

BIM adoption does not necessarily have to mean transforming every process overnight.

A practical approach can begin with the areas where better digital coordination is most valuable.

For example, a project team might initially focus on:

### 3D coordination

Bring architectural, structural and MEP information together to identify potential spatial conflicts.

### Clash detection

Identify coordination issues before they become physical problems on site.

### Model-based quantity information

Use structured model information to support quantity-related workflows where appropriate.

### 4D planning

Connect model information with construction sequencing and scheduling.

### Digital information management

Create a more structured way of organizing and sharing project information.

From there, BIM workflows can be expanded as the team gains experience and the project requires additional capabilities.

This staged approach can make BIM adoption easier to manage because the investment is connected to specific project requirements rather than technology for its own sake.

## The value of BIM goes beyond clash detection

Clash detection is often the first thing people associate with BIM.

It is certainly important, particularly on complex MEP projects, but it is only one part of the picture.

BIM can also support communication between stakeholders, visualization of design intent, construction planning, information management, quantity-related workflows, and eventually the management of information throughout the asset lifecycle.

A recent systematic review of 4D BIM literature identified benefits across visualization and communication, scheduling and planning, progress monitoring, and other areas of project delivery.

This broader view changes the conversation.

Instead of seeing BIM as an additional modelling expense, project teams can evaluate it as part of a wider **project information and coordination strategy**.

## How can companies make BIM adoption more practical?

For organizations concerned about budget, the solution may not be to avoid BIM entirely.

Instead, start by defining where it can create meaningful project value.

### 1. Assess project complexity

Consider the number of disciplines involved, the level of MEP services, design complexity, project duration, and coordination requirements.

### 2. Identify the highest-risk areas

Determine where design conflicts, revisions, coordination problems, or information gaps could have the biggest impact.

### 3. Choose the appropriate BIM scope

Not every project needs the same BIM workflow.

The required level of modelling, coordination, data and project information should be aligned with the project's actual requirements.

### 4. Build capability gradually

Companies can combine internal teams with external BIM specialists where appropriate rather than attempting to build every capability internally from day one.

### 5. Measure project outcomes

Instead of simply tracking the cost of BIM, track the outcomes it is intended to improve.

For example:

- Number of clashes identified before construction
- Design changes detected during coordination
- Rework avoided
- Coordination issues resolved
- RFIs related to coordination
- Time spent resolving design conflicts
- Schedule impacts associated with design changes

This creates a more meaningful basis for evaluating the investment.

## The bigger question for project leaders

BIM adoption should not be treated as a simple decision between **“use BIM”** and **“don't use BIM.”**

The better approach is to understand where digital coordination and structured project information can provide measurable value.

The construction industry is becoming increasingly digital, but successful adoption is not simply about buying technology. It requires people, processes, standards, communication, and a clear understanding of what the project actually needs.

For some projects, a limited BIM scope may be appropriate.

For others, especially complex projects involving multiple disciplines and significant coordination requirements, a more comprehensive BIM strategy may provide greater value.

The important thing is to make the decision based on **project needs rather than assumptions about cost alone**.

## From Cost Concern to Project Value

The hesitation around BIM is understandable.

Every project has budget limitations, and every technology investment should have a clear purpose.

But BIM should be evaluated in the context of the entire project lifecycle, not only by the cost of producing a model.

When better coordination can help teams identify issues earlier, communicate more effectively, organize project information, and support better-informed decisions, the discussion becomes broader than the price of BIM implementation.

The question is no longer simply, “Can we afford BIM?”

It becomes:

> **“Can we afford to manage complex projects without better coordination and information?”**

For project owners, consultants, contractors and engineering teams, that is a question worth asking before construction begins.

## Looking to adopt BIM?

TXG supports project teams with BIM and digital engineering solutions designed to improve coordination, information management, and project delivery.

**Talk to TXG about your next project and explore the BIM approach that fits your project requirements.**

title: Digital twins vs building management systems (BMS)
excerpt: Which is the Real Game Changer for Smart Infrastructure using BIM?
body:
Which is the Real Game Changer for Smart Infrastructure using BIM?

As smart buildings become increasingly complex, two powerful technologies stand at the forefront of intelligent infrastructure management: Digital Twins and Building Management Systems (BMS). Understanding the differences and how each contributes to smarter, more sustainable buildings is key to unlocking their full potential within the BIM ecosystem.

title: An introduction to Building Information Modelling (BIM)
excerpt: Building Information Modeling (BIM) is a revolutionary digital-first approach to planning, designing, constructing, and managing buildings and infrastructure.
body: Building Information Modeling (BIM) is a revolutionary digital-first approach to planning, designing, constructing, and managing buildings and infrastructure. Unlike traditional 2D drawings, BIM enables the creation of intelligent 3D models that integrate geometric, spatial, and real-time data, allowing for seamless collaboration across disciplines.

title: What is a digital twin?
excerpt: A Digital Twin is a dynamic, virtual representation of a physical asset, process, or system that continuously updates with real-time data from sensors, IoT devices, and other sources.
body: A Digital Twin is a dynamic, virtual representation of a physical asset, process, or system that continuously updates with real-time data from sensors, IoT devices, and other sources. This integration allows for simulation, predictive analysis, and optimization throughout the asset's lifecycle. Digital Twin technology revolutionizes the digital construction industry with real-time data integration and smarter decision-making. This technology bridges the gap between the digital and physical world, allowing construction professionals, architects, and facility managers to make informed decisions based on real-world performance data.
